reconnaissance_summary.censorship_and_self_censorship: The cited Freedom House, HRW, FCDO, OHCHR, State Department, and China Dissent Monitor materials document censorship, surveillance, detention, intimidation, restricted access, and substantial reporting asymmetry, especially for Xinjiang, Tibet, political dissent, nuclear command, and personal finances. Official denials and self-assessments are preserved as contrary evidence but are not independently verified.
chapter_specific_biases: 1B: capability estimates and official policy statements can be mistaken for implementation or personal command responsibility.
2B: military spending and UCDP zero observations establish capability or exposure, not restraint, legality, or non-initiation.
3B: NGO and external-government reporting makes visible abuses more observable, while closed-system silence suppresses contrary and remedy evidence.
4B: formal succession proves appointment, not contestability; visible protest and censorship create opposing observation biases.
5B: macroeconomic outcomes and official statistics do not identify distributional effects, policy ownership, or Xi-specific responsibility.
6B: long-run health and education gains and official protective measures must be separated from 2022 service quality, equity, and implementation.
7B: institutional corruption and disciplinary evidence must not be personalized; asset, family-benefit, and disclosure evidence remain opaque.
8B: administrative control and inspection capacity must not be equated with broad competence or successful public outcomes.
reconnaissance_summary.complaint_volume_interpretation: Complaint volume is not a reliable safety or integrity denominator in China. Open protest monitoring captures visible dissent but likely undercounts suppressed activity; absence of complaints, especially in closed regions or elite matters, is non-probative. Some documented concessions provide limited contrary evidence of administrative responsiveness.
reconnaissance_summary.criticism_possible: Independent criticism, NGO reporting, academic analysis, external-government assessments, reputable media, and limited domestic or online dissent were available. The cited sources also document that criticism carries substantial risk and that organized national opposition is not institutionally available.
reconnaissance_summary.duplicate_event_risk: High. E009–E013 and E071 overlap on repression and Xinjiang; E014–E017 and E056 overlap on political control and protest; E018–E021 and E059–E061 overlap on macroeconomic conditions; E022/E029/E048 share the Party Congress report; E054/E059/E062/E069/E075/E077 reuse the World Bank report; E026/E028/E066 share official anti-corruption reporting; E049/E050 overlap on Taiwan exercises. Same underlying facts must not be counted as independent confirmations.
reconnaissance_summary.inherited_conditions_shocks_and_authorit: The notebook distinguishes inherited nuclear posture, legal infrastructure, long-run economic and social trends, CCP institutional inheritance, and national administrative capacity from Xi-period formal authority and declared programs. Relevant shocks include COVID/zero-COVID, property contraction, slowing global demand, Russia’s invasion, Taiwan tensions, and the 2022 leadership transition. Personal attribution remains weaker than formal state or party authority attribution.
languages_and_archives_searched: English-language official Chinese government and MFA records
Chinese UN Mission and Chinese Embassy records
English-language OHCHR, FCDO, U.S. State Department, and DoD material
Freedom House, HRW, Amnesty, SIPRI, IMF, World Bank, UCDP, V-Dem, WGI, and related structured prior material
Reuters, Axios, Bloomberg, TIME, CSIS, Carnegie, Arms Control Association, APLN, and academic publications
reconnaissance_summary.official_statistics_reliability: Official Chinese economic, health, military, corruption, and administrative statistics are useful for reported policy and institutional activity but require corroboration. The notebook explicitly treats official self-assessments, disciplinary statistics, protective measures, and audit claims as limited or contextual where independent outcome verification is absent.
reconnaissance_summary.relevant_denominators: Country-level population, GDP, per-capita spending, conflict exposure, HDI, health, education, vaccination, political-freedom, corruption, and governance indicators are available in the local prior. Protest monitors report incident counts, but coverage is explicitly incomplete. No reliable denominator was found for hidden abuses, personal enrichment, family benefit, nuclear-control failures, proxy activity, or conditional service access.
reconnaissance_summary.safe_reporting_channels: External NGOs, intergovernmental assessments, academic studies, reputable international media, official diplomatic records, formal laws, and limited online or local grievance channels provided reporting routes. The cited sources document that domestic journalists, critics, protesters, victims, and civil-society organizations face censorship, detention, surveillance, or intimidation, so safe-channel coverage is incomplete.
reconnaissance_summary.source_concentration: The dossier uses multiple source families: OHCHR, IMF, World Bank, SIPRI, UCDP and WGI/V-Dem/Freedom House structured priors; HRW, Amnesty, Freedom House, FCDO, State Department; official Chinese records; DoD; Reuters, Axios, Bloomberg, TIME; CSIS, Carnegie, ACA, APLN; and academic research. Concentration remains material in human-rights, political-freedom, and COVID reporting, and official Chinese sources dominate favorable policy, safeguards, anti-corruption, and administrative-mechanism claims.
